title: Fusion and stars

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Main sequence
items.clue: The diagonal band on which about 90% of stars lie.

items.label: White dwarfs
items.clue: Hot but dim stars at the lower left, small in radius.

items.label: Hertzsprung–Russell (HR) diagram
items.clue: A graph of luminosity against surface temperature for stars.

items.label: Stellar equilibrium
items.clue: Inward gravity is balanced by outward gas and radiation pressure.

questions.stem: A main-sequence star stays the same size for millions of years. Which statement explains why it does not collapse?

options.text: Its rotation produces an outward centrifugal force on its gas that balances the inward pull of gravity.
No forces act on its gas at all, which is why the star is neither expanding nor contracting.
The inward gravitational forces on its gas are balanced by the outward radiation pressure maintained by fusion.
Gravity is negligible in space, so the hot gas of the star has no weight that needs supporting.

questions.explanation: In a stable star the inward gravitational force on each layer is balanced by the outward pressure maintained by the energy released in fusion in the core. The forces are large; it is their balance that keeps the size constant.

questions.stem: What is the source of the energy radiated by a main-sequence star such as the Sun?

options.text: Nuclear fusion of hydrogen into helium in its core
Chemical burning of hydrogen gas in oxygen, like a flame
Nuclear fission of heavy nuclei such as uranium and thorium
Heat left over from its formation, lost slowly as it cools

questions.explanation: In the core, hydrogen nuclei fuse to form helium-4. The products have less total rest mass than the reactants, and the difference is released as energy, E = Δmc².

questions.stem: Hydrogen fusion in a star needs a core temperature of the order of 10⁷ K. Why is such a high temperature needed?

options.text: Fusion absorbs energy, and the thermal energy of the core supplies it.
Hydrogen must reach its ignition temperature before it can burn.
Nuclei need enough energy to overcome the strong nuclear force.
Nuclei must move fast enough to overcome electric repulsion.

questions.explanation: Nuclei are positively charged and repel. Only at very high temperatures do enough nuclei move fast enough to approach within about 10⁻¹⁵ m, where the attractive strong nuclear force can bind them.

questions.stem: Star X has a mass of 10 M⊙ and star Y a mass of 1 M⊙; both are main-sequence stars. X has about ten times as much hydrogen available for fusion as Y, but it is about 3000 times as luminous. How does the main-sequence lifetime of X compare with that of Y?

options.text: About 10 times as long as Y's
About the same length as Y's
About 1/300 as long as Y's
About 1/3000 as long as Y's

questions.explanation: Lifetime ∝ (fuel available)/(rate of use) ∝ fuel/L. For X relative to Y this is 10/3000 = 3.3 × 10⁻³ ≈ 1/300: X has more hydrogen, but it uses it far faster.

questions.stem: An HR diagram is drawn with luminosity on the vertical axis (increasing upwards) and surface temperature on the horizontal axis (decreasing to the right). The main sequence is a band running from the upper left to the lower right. Which statement about main-sequence stars is correct?

options.text: Their position on the band is set mainly by mass: more massive stars lie higher up.
Each star moves steadily along the band, from upper left to lower right, as it ages.
They all have about the same radius as the Sun, as they form a single narrow band.
Those at the upper left last longest, since they have the most hydrogen to fuse.

questions.stem: Two measurements of the position of a nearby star against very distant background stars, made six months apart, differ by an angle of 0.0700 arc-second. Take 1 pc = 3.09 × 10¹⁶ m, 1 ly = 9.46 × 10¹⁵ m and 1 AU = 1.50 × 10¹¹ m. What is the distance to the star in AU?

An HR diagram is drawn with luminosity on the vertical axis (increasing upwards) and surface temperature on the horizontal axis (decreasing to the right). A red giant on the diagram has a luminosity of 100 L⊙ and a surface temperature of 4000 K. A white dwarf has a luminosity of 0.010 L⊙ and a surface temperature of 16 000 K. Both are modelled as black bodies. What is (radius of the red giant)/(radius of the white dwarf)?
In the core of a star, hydrogen fusion stops when the hydrogen there has been used up. What happens to the core next, and why?

options.text: It stays the same size and simply cools down, like a fire that has gone out once its fuel is used up.
It explodes at once as a supernova, because a star blows itself apart as soon as its fuel has run out.
It contracts, because the helium made by fusion has made the core more massive, so its gravity is now stronger than before.
It contracts, because without fusion the outward radiation pressure no longer balances the inward gravitational force.

questions.explanation: Fusion maintained the outward pressure that balanced gravity. When it stops, the pressure falls, the resultant force is inwards and the core contracts. The contraction heats the core, which leads to the next stage of the star's evolution.

questions.stem: One reaction in the Sun's core is ³He + ³He → ⁴He + 2 ¹H. The atomic masses are 3.016029 u for helium-3, 4.002603 u for helium-4 and 1.007825 u for hydrogen-1 (the electron masses balance). Take 1 u = 1.661 × 10⁻²⁷ kg and c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. How much energy is released in one reaction?

At the centre of the Sun the temperature is about 1.5 × 10⁷ K and the density about 1.5 × 10⁵ kg m⁻³. Fusion takes place only in this central core. How, if at all, does the very high density affect fusion in the core?

options.text: It makes collisions between nuclei frequent enough for fusion to release energy at a high rate.
It brings nuclei close enough together for the gravity between them to pull them into each other.
It has no effect on fusion; only the high temperature of the core affects the rate of fusion.
It gives each nucleus more kinetic energy, which it needs to overcome electric repulsion.

questions.stem: Which sequence of stages describes the evolution of a star of 1 M⊙, such as the Sun, after it forms?

options.text: Main sequence → red giant → supernova explosion
Main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
Main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → black hole
Main sequence → white dwarf → red giant → red supergiant

questions.explanation: When core hydrogen is used up, a 1 M⊙ star swells into a red giant. Its core never gets hot enough for fusion beyond carbon and oxygen; the outer layers are shed as a planetary nebula and the exposed core becomes a white dwarf.

questions.stem: An HR diagram is drawn with luminosity on the vertical axis (increasing upwards) and surface temperature on the horizontal axis (decreasing to the right). Stars A and B lie on the same line of constant radius. A has a surface temperature of 9000 K and B a surface temperature of 6000 K. Both are modelled as black bodies. What is the ratio (luminosity of A)/(luminosity of B)?
questions.explanation: On a line of constant radius, L = σ4πR²T⁴ with R the same, so L_A/L_B = (T_A/T_B)⁴ = (9000/6000)⁴ = 1.5⁴ = 5.1. The hotter star lies higher up the line, to the left.
